svg.title: Progestins and meningioma: absolute risk per 100,000 person-years, the relative multiples, and the one ingredient still licensed in Taiwan
svg.desc: Schematic: progestins and meningioma, with absolute risk and relative risk held in one frame. The top of the figure settles the biggest misunderstanding first: combined oral contraceptives show no association, tagged "Observational meta-analysis, no significant association", the headline figure being a relative risk of 0.93 with a 95 per cent confidence interval of 0.83 to 1.03, from a meta-analysis of 12 case-control and 6 cohort studies; so "taking the pill gives you a meningioma" does not stand up in the evidence. Beside it, pointing the other way, is menopausal hormone therapy: in the same meta-analysis a relative risk of 1.19 (1.01 to 1.40), and 1.32 (1.07 to 1.64) in postmenopausal women; and in a separate meta-analysis of menopausal hormone therapy alone - 11 studies, 1,820,954 people, 3,249 meningiomas - a pooled odds ratio of 1.29 (1.03 to 1.60), with 1.27 in current users, significant, and 1.12 in past users, not significant, the authors writing that whether the association is causal is for later research to establish. The second section is headed "For the ingredients that do carry a signal, this is what the absolute risk looks like", tagged "Per 100,000 person-years, French national health insurance cohorts", and states the outcome definition first: in all of these studies the outcome is surgery or radiotherapy for an intracranial meningioma, not being diagnosed with a meningioma. Each of three ingredients is drawn as a pair of horizontal bars, exposed above and not exposed below, on one shared per-100,000 person-years scale. Cyproterone acetate at high dose, a cohort study in France of more than 250,000 girls and women aged 7 to 70, exposure defined as a cumulative 3 g or more in the first six months: 23.8 cases among the exposed against 4.5 among the unexposed, adjusted 6.6 times (4.0 to 11.1), and above a cumulative 60 g the multiple rises to 21.7 (10.8 to 43.5). Nomegestrol acetate, a French cohort of more than 1.06 million women: 19.3 against 7.0, age-adjusted 2.9 times (2.4 to 3.7), and above a cumulative 6 g the multiple rises to 12.0 (9.9 to 16.0). Chlormadinone acetate, a French cohort of more than 820,000 people: 18.5 against 6.8, 3.1 times (2.4 to 4.0), and above a cumulative 8.64 g the rate approaches 47 per 100,000 person-years. Every multiple sits against its own absolute risk; none appears on its own. The section closes with a passage noting that at the highest point, 23.8 per 100,000 person-years works out at roughly 2.4 in 10,000 for one person in one year; that the European Medicines Agency puts it the same way, calling the side effect rare and affecting roughly 1 to 10 people in every 10,000 depending on dose and duration, with risk rising with cumulative dose; and that the multiple is alarming while the baseline is low, so both have to be held in mind at once. The third section is three columns - signal present, no signal, insufficient data - from a French national case-control study of 18,061 people who had surgery for an intracranial meningioma between 2009 and 2018, matched 1:5 by year of birth and place of residence to 90,305 controls. Signal present: medrogestone, odds ratio 3.49 (2.38 to 5.10); injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate 5.55 (2.27 to 13.56); promegestone 2.39 (1.85 to 3.09), with these excess risks driven by use of more than one year; and the three already known to carry risk read, in the same dataset, cyproterone 19.21 (16.61 to 22.22), nomegestrol 4.93 and chlormadinone 3.87. No signal: progesterone, dydrogesterone and the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system. Insufficient data: dienogest and hydroxyprogesterone, too few users to draw a conclusion. Beneath the columns the 2026 meta-analysis pulls the picture together: cyproterone acetate, pooled odds ratio 12.36 (7.47 to 20.45), moderate certainty; depot injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.68 (1.72 to 4.19), low certainty; and the authors' own assessment that observational design, residual confounding, heterogeneity and imprecision in some exposures all limit the strength of the evidence. The fourth section gives the population-level figures after stopping, explicitly labelled as data and not as an instruction: for nomegestrol, one year or more after stopping, risk was the same as in the unexposed group, 1.0 (0.8 to 1.3); for cyproterone, one year after stopping, risk was still 1.8 times that of the unexposed group (1.0 to 3.2), clearly down but not all the way back to baseline. The fifth section is Taiwan: of the three ingredients only one is still available. From a record-by-record search of all 72,043 entries in the TFDA full medicinal product licence dataset - cyproterone acetate has several currently valid licences; nomegestrol acetate has one record in the whole dataset, revoked, valid until 15 January 2020; chlormadinone acetate likewise one record, revoked; medrogestone and promegestone have no current records; and all current medroxyprogesterone acetate licences are oral formulations, the injectable formulation having been revoked with validity ending 9 May 2020. The same panel carries TFDA announcement Wei-Shou-Shi No. 1111407692 of 15 September 2022, which under Article 48 of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act requires the Chinese-language package insert of high-dose 50 mg cyproterone-containing products to add to the contraindications section, quoted verbatim, "patients who currently have, or have a history of, meningioma"; to add meningioma-related safety information to the "Warnings and Precautions" and "Pharmacological Properties" sections; to change the indication to "for use only where there is no other treatment option, or where other treatments have been ineffective"; and to add to the dosage section that once clinical symptoms have improved, the lowest effective dose should be used to maintain the effect - the low-dose 2 mg products carrying the same additions. At the foot of the figure is a panel headed "Who to take this question back to". It begins with what not to do: do not stop the medicine on your own, since whether to stop or change it is a decision for the doctor who prescribed it and has to be weighed together with why it was prescribed in the first place. Then four things to ask: take the medicine packet back to the department that prescribed it and establish which ingredient it actually is, reading the English ingredient name rather than the brand name; ask how long it was taken and roughly what the cumulative dose comes to; ask whether a brain magnetic resonance scan is warranted given the current situation; and if stopping is decided on, whether to repeat the scan three months later to see the trend. The last line is for people who already have a meningioma: the association between these medicines and meningioma comes entirely from observational data, and the outcome measured is a meningioma severe enough to need surgery or radiotherapy, so what it tells you is that the question is worth taking to a doctor, not that the medicine caused your tumour.

g.text: PROGESTINS AND MENINGIOMA - ABSOLUTE RISK AND RELATIVE RISK IN ONE FRAME
Progestins and meningioma: an alarming multiple on a very
low baseline
The first thing to settle is which ingredient was taken. The clear signals belong to a few specific progestins, not to the phrase
"the pill".
Every multiple on this figure sits beside its own absolute risk; a relative risk is never shown on its own. All of this is
observational data, and association is not causation - and nothing on this figure says "so stop taking it".
First, the biggest misunderstanding: combined oral contraceptives show no association
Observational meta-analysis, no significant association
Relative risk 0.93 (95% confidence interval
Meta-analysis of 12 case-control and 6 cohort studies. Relative risk divides the probability
of the event in one group by that in the other. [B-S49]
So "taking the pill gives you a meningioma" does not stand up in the
evidence. The clear signals belong to other ingredients.
Menopausal hormone therapy in the same analysis and one other (the
direction is the opposite, so it belongs here too)
In the same meta-analysis, menopausal hormone therapy carried a relative risk
of 1.19 (1.01 to 1.40), and 1.32 (1.07 to 1.64) in postmenopausal women. [B-S49]
A separate meta-analysis of menopausal hormone therapy alone (11 studies,
1,820,954 people, 3,249 meningiomas) gives a pooled odds ratio of 1.29 (1.03 to
1.60), with 1.27 in current users, significant, and 1.12 in past users, not
significant. The authors write that whether the association is causal is for later
research to establish. [B-S50]
An odds ratio divides one ratio of events to non-events by another; it is not a
multiple of a probability.
For the ingredients that do carry a signal, this is what the absolute risk looks like
Per 100,000 person-years, French national health insurance cohorts
In all of these studies the outcome is defined as "surgery or radiotherapy for an intracranial meningioma", not "diagnosed with a meningioma" - so what is
measured is the part severe enough to need treatment, and it sits below the true prevalence. [B-S42] [B-S43] [B-S44]
Cyproterone acetate (high dose)
Cohort study, France, more than 250,000 girls and women aged 7 to 70; exposure defined as a cumulative 3 g or more in the first six months
Exposed
Not exposed
Adjusted 6.6 times (4.0 to 11.1)
Above a cumulative 60 g, the multiple rises to 21.7 (10.8 to 43.5). [B-S42]
Nomegestrol acetate
Cohort study, France, more than 1.06 million women
Exposed
Not exposed
Age-adjusted 2.9 times (2.4 to 3.7)
Above a cumulative 6 g, the multiple rises to 12.0 (9.9 to 16.0). [B-S43]
Chlormadinone acetate
Cohort study, France, more than 820,000 people
Exposed
Not exposed
Above a cumulative 8.64 g, the rate approaches 47 per 100,000 person-years. [B-S44]
Meningiomas treated with surgery or radiotherapy, per 100,000 person-years
Three ingredients, one shape: the longer the use and the larger the cumulative dose, the wider the gap.
Setting the absolute numbers out is worth doing
At the highest point, 23.8 per 100,000 person-years works out at roughly 2.4 in 10,000 for one person in one year.
The European Medicines Agency puts it the same way: this side effect is rare, affecting roughly 1 to 10 people in every 10,000 depending on dose and duration of
use, and the risk rises with cumulative dose. [B-S55]
The multiple is alarming and the baseline is low. Both have to be held in mind at once.
The other half of the answer: which ingredients carry a signal and which do not
A French national case-control study: 18,061 people who had surgery for an intracranial meningioma between 2009 and 2018, matched 1:5 by year of birth and place of
residence to 90,305 controls. An odds ratio is not a multiple of a probability. [B-S45]
Signal present
Excess risk, driven by use of more than one year
Medrogestone
Odds ratio 3.49 (2.38 to 5.10)
Injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate
Promegestone
The three already known to carry risk read, in the
same dataset, cyproterone 19.21 (16.61 to 22.22),
nomegestrol 4.93 and chlormadinone 3.87.
No signal
No excess risk seen in this dataset
Progesterone
Dydrogesterone
Levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system
The 2026 meta-analysis also places levonorgestrel and
progesterone in the no-signal group. [B-S46]
Insufficient data
Too few users to draw a conclusion
Dienogest
Hydroxyprogesterone
The 2026 meta-analysis places chlormadinone,
nomegestrol, promegestone, medrogestone and
desogestrel in a further group: a signal is present, but
the data are sparse and heterogeneity high, so they
were not pooled. [B-S46]
The 2026 meta-analysis pulls the overall picture together
Cyproterone acetate, pooled odds ratio 12.36 (7.47 to 20.45), moderate certainty of evidence.
Depot injectable medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.68 (1.72 to 4.19), low certainty.
The authors' own assessment of overall certainty: observational design, residual confounding, heterogeneity and imprecision in some exposures all limit the
strength of the evidence. (78 studies reviewed, 14 pooled.) [B-S46]
Population-level figures after stopping (this is data, not an instruction)
Nomegestrol
One year or more after stopping, risk was the same as in the unexposed
Cyproterone
One year after stopping, risk was still 1.8 times that of the unexposed group
(1.0 to 3.2) - clearly down, but not all the way back to baseline. [B-S42]
These two lines are population-level observations. They are not a medication instruction for anyone.
In Taiwan: of the three ingredients, only one is still available
TFDA full medicinal product licence dataset, all 72,043 records searched
Cyproterone acetate
Still available
Several licences currently valid
Nomegestrol acetate
Licence revoked
One record in the whole dataset, revoked, valid until 15 January 2020
Chlormadinone acetate
Licence revoked
Also one record only, revoked
Medrogestone, promegestone
No current records
No current records
Medroxyprogesterone acetate
Injectable revoked
All current licences are oral formulations; the injectable formulation is revoked, valid
until 9 May 2020
Most of the ingredients carrying the highest risk in the French studies are not
obtainable by a reader in Taiwan. The one that remains is cyproterone.
And the Taiwanese package insert says so, because the regulator
ordered it added
TFDA announcement Wei-Shou-Shi No. 1111407692 of 15 September 2022, under Article 48
of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act, requires the Chinese-language package insert of
high-dose (50 mg) cyproterone-containing products - and equally of the low-dose (2 mg)
products - to:
add to the CONTRAINDICATIONS section: "patients who currently
have, or have a history of, meningioma"
add meningioma-related safety information to the "Warnings and Precautions"
and "Pharmacological Properties" sections;
change the indication to "for use only where there is no other treatment option,
or where other treatments have been ineffective";
add to the dosage section: "once clinical symptoms have improved, the lowest
effective dose should be used to maintain the effect". [B-S53]
Who to take this question back to
First, what not to do: do not stop the medicine on your own. Whether to stop it or change it is a decision for the doctor who prescribed it, and it has to be
weighed together with why it was prescribed in the first place - hirsutism, acne, endometriosis, menopausal symptoms all have different alternatives,
and the original problem does not disappear when the medicine does.
Take the medicine packet back to
the department that prescribed it
The first thing to establish is which ingredient it actually is. Read the English ingredient name on the packet, not the brand name.
Then ask about exposure
How long it was taken, and roughly what the cumulative dose comes to.
Then ask about imaging
Given the current situation, is a brain magnetic resonance scan warranted.
If stopping is decided on
Whether to repeat the scan three months later to see the trend.
A last word for people who already have a meningioma: the association between these medicines and meningioma comes entirely from observational
data, and the outcome measured is "a meningioma severe enough to need surgery or radiotherapy". What it tells you is that the question is worth taking
to a doctor - not that this medicine caused your tumour.
Schematic, redrawn from the meta-analysis of reproductive and exogenous hormone factors (Qi 2013), the meta-analysis of menopausal hormone therapy (Fan
2013), the French cyproterone acetate cohort (Weill 2021), the nomegestrol acetate cohort (Nguyen 2024), the chlormadinone acetate cohort (Roland 2025), the
national case-control study (Roland 2024), the progestin meta-analysis (Hudelist 2026), the European Medicines Agency statement (2020), and the Taiwanese TFDA
licence dataset and announcement of 15 September 2022; the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be
compared directly.
